Sensitivity to an Omitted Confounder in Multilevel Mediation

RMediation Development Team

Source: vignettes/omitted-confounder-sensitivity.Rmd
omitted-confounder-sensitivity.Rmd

What the function does

A mediation estimate is only as credible as the assumption that nothing unmeasured confounds the mediator-outcome relation. ml_omitted_confounder() asks how much that assumption could matter in a two-level (1-1-1) design: treatment A, mediator M and outcome Y are all measured at level 1, and the effects are split into a between-cluster and a within-cluster part. It follows Tofighi and Kelley (2016).

You describe a hypothetical standardized confounder Z by three correlations:

Parameter Meaning
r_za correlation of Z with the treatment
r_zm correlation of Z with the mediator
r_zy correlation of Z with the outcome

For each combination on a grid, the function returns the indirect effect after adjusting the a path and the b path for Z: a = a* - d_MZ * d_ZA and b = b* - d_YZ * s_ZM, where a* and b* are your unadjusted estimates. The adjusted indirect effect is a * b.

Inputs

For each level, supply the two unadjusted paths and the covariance matrix of A, M and Y at that level (or the correlation matrix and standard deviations):

ml_omitted_confounder(
  between = list(a = 0.3, b = 0.4, cov = S_between),
  within  = list(a = 0.2, b = 0.5, cov = S_within),
  r_za = c(0, 0.1, 0.3)
)

Rows and columns follow var_order (default c("A", "M", "Y")). Supply at least one level.

A small example 

R <- matrix(c(1, .3, .2,
              .3, 1, .4,
              .2, .4, 1), 3)
res <- ml_omitted_confounder(
  between = list(a = 0.3, b = 0.4, cor = R, sd = c(1, 1, 1)),
  r_za = c(0, 0.1)
)
res
#> Omitted-confounder sensitivity (Tofighi & Kelley, 2016)
#> =======================================================
#> Unadjusted indirect effect:
#>   between 0.1200
#> Screen: pd 
#>   Points with a non-positive-definite augmented matrix are NA; use
#>   screen = "none" to reproduce the published tables.
#> Adjusted indirect effect by level and r_za:
#>   between r_za = 0    ab_adj 0.0488 to 0.2761 (admitted 10201 of 10201)
#>   between r_za = 0.1  ab_adj 0.0441 to 0.3463 (admitted 10201 of 10201)
#> Assumption: the covariance of the level-2 random slopes of a and b is zero.

summary() adds, for each panel, how many grid points reverse the sign of the indirect effect and the weakest confounder (smallest r_zm^2 + r_zy^2) that does so:

invisible(summary(res))
#> Omitted-confounder sensitivity: summary
#> Ranges of the adjusted indirect effect:
#>    level r_za     min    max argmin_r_zm argmin_r_zy argmax_r_zm argmax_r_zy
#>  between  0.0 0.04882 0.2761        -0.5        -0.5         0.5        -0.5
#>  between  0.1 0.04411 0.3463        -0.5        -0.5        -0.5         0.5
#>  n_admitted n_total
#>       10201   10201
#>       10201   10201
#> 
#> Points where the adjusted effect changes sign relative to the unadjusted effect
#> (weakest = flipping point with the smallest r_zm^2 + r_zy^2):
#>    level r_za n_flip share_flip weakest_r_zm weakest_r_zy
#>  between  0.0      0          0           NA           NA
#>  between  0.1      0          0           NA           NA

plot() draws the adjusted indirect effect over the r_zm by r_zy grid, with the zero contour; type = "region" also draws the boundary of the admissible region:

plot(res, r_za = 0.1, type = "region")

as.data.frame(res) returns the full grid for your own summaries.

Reproducing the published example

Tofighi and Kelley’s supplementary materials print the between and within covariance estimates of the empirical example, in the order m, y, x, to three decimals. Passing var_order = c("M", "Y", "A") tells the function that order.

SW <- matrix(c(.351, .167, .062,
               .167, .474, .096,
               .062, .096, .793), 3)
SB <- matrix(c(.649, .475, -.001,
               .475, .526, -.024,
               -.001, -.024, .207), 3)
paper <- ml_omitted_confounder(
  between = list(a = 0.024, b = 0.784, cov = SB),
  within  = list(a = 0.086, b = 0.433, cov = SW),
  r_za = c(0, 0.1, 0.3), screen = "none",
  var_order = c("M", "Y", "A")
)
printed <- data.frame(
  printed_min = c(.017, -.087, -.372, .017, .011, -.016),
  printed_max = c(.032, .152, .447, .085, .121, .226)
)
knitr::kable(
  cbind(paper@ranges[, c("level", "r_za", "min", "max")], printed),
  digits = 4
)
level r_za min max printed_min printed_max
between 0.0 0.0170 0.0319 0.017 0.032
between 0.1 -0.0872 0.1518 -0.087 0.152
between 0.3 -0.3729 0.4462 -0.372 0.447
within 0.0 0.0168 0.0846 0.017 0.085
within 0.1 0.0111 0.1210 0.011 0.121
within 0.3 -0.0161 0.2258 -0.016 0.226

The computed endpoints agree with the printed ones to within about 0.001; the remaining differences come from the three-decimal rounding of the published covariances.

Things to know

  • The default screen is stricter than the paper. A grid point is admissible only when the augmented correlation matrix of A, M, Y and Z is positive definite, equivalently r2 < 1 in the returned grid. With screen = "pd" (the default) other points are NA. The published endpoints cover the whole grid, so reproducing them needs screen = "none". With the example above, the default shrinks the between-level ranges:
pd <- ml_omitted_confounder(
  between = list(a = 0.024, b = 0.784, cov = SB),
  r_za = 0.3, var_order = c("M", "Y", "A")
)
none <- ml_omitted_confounder(
  between = list(a = 0.024, b = 0.784, cov = SB),
  r_za = 0.3, screen = "none", var_order = c("M", "Y", "A")
)
rbind(
  pd   = unlist(pd@ranges[, c("min", "max", "n_admitted", "n_total")]),
  none = unlist(none@ranges[, c("min", "max", "n_admitted", "n_total")])
)
#>             min       max n_admitted n_total
#> pd   -0.2957761 0.3475489       8289   10201
#> none -0.3728657 0.4462128       8289   10201
  • Your a and b need not equal the covariance-implied values. The published example does not. The function subtracts a covariance-derived bias term from the values you supply; it does not refit anything.
  • The covariance between the level-2 random slopes of a and b is taken to be zero, as in the published illustration.
  • Singular points return NA, and a panel with no admissible points has NA ranges and n_admitted = 0.
  • This is a sensitivity analysis, not an estimate. It shows how large a confounder would have to be to change a conclusion; it cannot tell you whether such a confounder exists.

Reference

Tofighi, D., & Kelley, K. (2016). Assessing omitted confounder bias in multilevel mediation models. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(1), 86-105. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2015.1105736
